We are a team of passionate STEM students from Uzbekistan.

Our team brings experience in mechanical engineering, Python programming, machine learning, robotics, and web development. We aim to develop an innovative, practical, and scientifically grounded solution using NASA's open data.

We value teamwork, curiosity, and the willingness to experiment with new ideas. We are interested in collaborating with people skilled in software development, data analysis, UI/UX design, and space science.
summary: LunaWindow helps users answer three connected questions: where, when, and why should a lunar mission operate? Built for the Lunar Landing Site Navigator challenge, our browser-based tool combines NASA JPL Horizons Sun/Earth geometry with LRO LOLA terrain to compare landing locations and find mission windows that meet user-defined sunlight, Earth-visibility, darkness, and blackout requirements. Users can explore the Moon, compare sites, inspect slope and roughness on three detailed south-pole terrain crops, and experience the selected place and time from the surface. Explainable rankings show why a window meets or misses each requirement, while shareable scenarios and downloadable reports make results reproducible. NASA illumination, permanent-shadow, Diviner thermal, and ShadowCam resources provide additional context. LunaWindow makes complex lunar data accessible to students, educators, and early mission-concept teams, with visible sources, coverage limits, and uncertainty. It supports preliminary exploration and screening; it does not certify landing safety or communications performance.
details:
LunaWindow: Lunar Landing Site Navigator

THE PROBLEM AND OUR APPROACH: Near the lunar south pole, a ridge can hide the low Sun and interrupt solar power. Earth visibility also changes with lunar libration. Choosing a location without considering timing and local terrain can miss these trade-offs. LunaWindow connects site selection, mission timing, terrain screening, and an observer's surface view in one accessible browser application.

WHAT USERS CAN DO: Explore & Compare lets users select from 19 cited locations or choose custom coordinates on a rotatable Moon. Synchronized charts, visibility timelines, and comparison metrics show sunlight, Earth visibility, simultaneous visibility, and the longest interruptions. The Mission Window Finder searches dates using the user's mission duration and hard requirements, then ranks candidates using transparent preference weights. “Why this window?” explains each result with the actual modeled values. A shared scenario links the workspaces and can be exported as JSON or a printable mission summary.

The 3D Terrain workspace supports detailed comparisons at Connecting Ridge, Shackleton Rim, and Nobile Rim 1. NASA LOLA 5 m gridded elevation supports derived slope and detrended RMS roughness screening within a selected footprint; a coarser 20 m mesh is used for display. Optional permanent-shadow, Diviner temperature/ice-stability, and ShadowCam layers are explicitly identified as models or observations. Surface View connects the numerical results to a 360-degree horizon panorama and, on the three processed terrain crops, a first-person 3D view with the Sun and Earth at their modeled bearings and angular sizes.

HOW IT WORKS AND NASA DATA: A Python pipeline prepares JPL Horizons DE441 Sun/Earth geometry in the Moon-fixed frame, LOLA terrain horizons, and source-attributed scientific layers. The application covers 2023–2031. Terrain-aware visibility compares the upper edge of each disc with the local terrain horizon; a separate geometric-horizon mode makes the terrain effect visible. Hourly samples produce whole-hour durations and one-hour rise/set windows. NASA GSFC PGDA illumination products provide independent reference comparisons. The repository documents validation against JPL topocentric geometry and source terrain data, plus reproducible unit and browser checks.

BENEFITS AND CREATIVITY: The project turns separate astronomy and terrain datasets into an understandable “where, when, and why” workflow. Users can trace a recommendation back to a requirement, a chart, the obstructing horizon, and the surface view. This can support education, public engagement, and early mission-concept screening while making trade-offs and missing data visible.

TOOLS: TypeScript, React APIs with a Preact production runtime, Three.js, Vite, SVG/canvas visualization, and Python data processing with NumPy, rasterio, pyproj, SciPy, and requests. Vitest and Playwright support testing. The static website is hosted on GitHub Pages. Source, methods, validation, data inventory, and software/font credits are available at https://github.com/Muxsinjon/ultimate_luna.

LIMITATIONS: This is a preliminary decision-support prototype, not an official NASA product or a landing-safety certification. Detailed terrain screening is limited to three processed crops; custom/global terrain is coarser. A 5 m grid is not equivalent to independent measurements every 5 m. DEM interpolation, sampling, terrain coverage, and uncertainty limit results. Geometric Earth visibility is not a communications link budget, and Diviner ice-stability context is not a detection of ice. User-selected thresholds are illustrative constraints, not NASA engineering standards. Optional sites flagged for coordinate verification should not be described as independently verified.

AI / SUPER INTELLIGENCE DISCLOSURE: Anthropic Claude and OpenAI Codex assisted with implementation, debugging, tests, data-processing scripts, research, interface design, documentation, and submission wording under team direction. The team selected the concept and approach. Scientific values are calculated from attributed NASA/JPL data rather than invented by AI. The repository's AI_USAGE.md, application metadata, and exported scenario metadata record AI assistance. Visual assets rendered by AI-assisted code are distinguished from scientific observations; the project share image carries a visible disclosure.
